Class SpeedOfLightLatency

java.lang.Object
com.eqixiac.equinix.design.geo.SpeedOfLightLatency
public final class SpeedOfLightLatency extends Object
Estimates network latency from geographic distance using the speed of light in optical fiber.

Light in glass fiber travels at c / n, where n ≈ 1.467 is the refractive index — roughly 204,000 km/s, or ~4.9 µs per km one-way. The estimate is:

one-way ms = distanceKm * routeFactor / (c / n / 1000)

and round-trip is twice that. routeFactor (default 1.0) inflates the great-circle distance for non-direct fibre paths; leave it at 1.0 for the theoretical speed-of-light floor, or set ~1.3–1.5 for a realistic terrestrial route. The result is a physical lower bound (or estimate) — it excludes switching, queuing, and serialization delay.

The round-trip (RTT) mode is the default, since RTT is what most latency budgets are quoted in.

Latency is computed IBX-to-IBX — between two specific Equinix data centers using each IBX's own coordinates — not between metro centroids, so two IBXes in the same metro have a real (small, non-zero) distance.

Endpoint types

Latency can be computed between any mix of the SDK's location-bearing types:

  • IBX ↔ IBX — millisBetween(Ibx, Ibx): the most precise figure, using each data center's own coordinates (from internetAccess.ibxs()); two IBXes in the same metro get a real, small, non-zero distance.
  • Metro ↔ Metro — millisBetween(Metro, Metro): metro-centroid figure using Fabric's metro coordinates (from fabric.metros() / fabric.metroRegistry()). Fine for city-to-city planning; same-metro pairs compute as 0.
  • IBX ↔ Metro — millisBetween(Ibx, Metro) / millisBetween(Metro, Ibx): mixed precision, e.g. "from my cage in LA4 to the Dallas metro".
  • Raw — millisBetween(GeoCoordinate, GeoCoordinate), distanceKm(double, double, double, double) and millisForKm(double) for arbitrary coordinates or known distances, fully offline.

Coordinates are optional in both source APIs, so every typed overload throws IllegalArgumentException naming the offending IBX/metro when coordinates are missing — fail loud rather than return a bogus zero.

For metro-to-metro, compare the calculated floor against Equinix's measured inter-metro RTT: metro.getConnectedMetros() carries avgLatency (ms) observed on the Fabric backbone. The floor tells you what physics allows; avgLatency tells you what the network delivers.

Ibx la4 = internetAccess.ibxs().getByCode("LA4");
Ibx sv5 = internetAccess.ibxs().getByCode("SV5");
Metro dc = fabric.metros().getByMetroCode(MetroCode.DC);
Metro sv = fabric.metros().getByMetroCode(MetroCode.SV);

SpeedOfLightLatency rtt = SpeedOfLightLatency.roundTrip();   // default
double ibxToIbx     = rtt.millisBetween(la4, sv5);           // precise, IBX-to-IBX
double metroToMetro = rtt.millisBetween(dc, sv);             // metro centroids
double ibxToMetro   = rtt.millisBetween(la4, dc);            // mixed

SpeedOfLightLatency realistic = SpeedOfLightLatency.builder()
        .mode(Mode.ONE_WAY).routeFactor(1.4).build();
double oneWay = realistic.millisForKm(1000);                 // ~6.85 ms
